10.html:
Hardenability is the ability of a steel to form martensite to a depth on quenching (measured as the ideal critical diameter D_I or by the Jominy curve). Anything that delays the diffusional austenite to ferrite, pearlite or bainite reactions, moving the TTT nose to the right, raises it.

Factors

  1. Carbon dissolved in austenite, first of all: it sets the martensite hardness (\mathrm{HRC_{99.9}} = 35 + 50\,\%\mathrm{C}) and slows the ferrite and pearlite reactions. Only carbon dissolved at austenitising counts.
  2. Dissolved alloying elements: all except Co retard the reactions, because they must partition and diffuse slowly. Grossmann: D_I = D_{I,\mathrm{base}} \times f_{\mathrm{Mn}} \times f_{\mathrm{Si}} \times \dots; for 0.25C-0.3Si-0.7Mn-1.1Cr-0.2Mo at ASTM 7, D_I = 0.17 \times 1.2 \times 3.3 \times 3.4 \times 1.6 = 3.7 in. B (0.0015 to 0.003%) is very potent in low-C steel.
  3. Austenite grain size: coarse grains offer less boundary area for ferrite and pearlite nucleation, so hardenability rises, at the cost of toughness and cracking.
  4. Undissolved carbides and inhomogeneity: they withdraw C and alloy and nucleate pearlite, lowering hardenability; austenitising time and temperature must dissolve them.
  5. Section size and shape: larger sections cool more slowly at the centre; at equal thickness a plate or rectangular bar hardens less deep than a round bar, because heat leaves its centre in fewer directions.
  6. Quench medium and agitation (severity H: still oil about 0.3, still water 1, still brine 2, higher with agitation): these fix the actual depth (D_{\mathrm{crit}}), not D_I.

Ranking (highest to lowest): C > Mn > Mo > Cr > Si > Ni.

  • C comes first because it controls both the attainable hardness and the depth.
  • Multiplying factors at 0.5 wt% (slide 27): Mn 2.7, Mo 2.5, Cr 2.1, Si 1.35, Ni 1.2.
  • Ni is weak alone and is used with Cr and Mo for toughness (4340).

11.html:
Why Mn. The matrix of grey iron is decided at the eutectoid. Austenite can follow the stable reaction, \gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \text{graphite}, where carbon diffuses to the nearby flakes and leaves ferrite, or the metastable reaction, \gamma \rightarrow \alpha + \mathrm{Fe_3C}, which gives pearlite. The 1 to 3% Si of grey iron and slow cooling favour the stable reaction, so the iron tends to ferrite. Mn is the cheap, controllable element that tips the balance to pearlite without the heavy chill of Cr: grey irons range from about 0.1% Mn (ferritic) to 1.2% Mn (pearlitic) (slide 6).

Mechanism:

  1. S is neutralised first. S as FeS promotes cementite. Mn has a higher affinity for S and forms MnS, \%\mathrm{Mn} = 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S}, so only the free Mn controls pearlite (slide 4): 1.7\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.15 gives maximum ferrite and 3\,\%\mathrm{S} + 0.35 a pearlitic matrix.
  2. Cementite is stabilised. Free Mn dissolves in cementite as (\mathrm{Fe,Mn})_3\mathrm{C} and resists its breakdown to graphite.
  3. Carbon stays in the matrix. Mn raises the carbon solubility in austenite and the combined carbon (book p 296), so less carbon migrates to the flakes.
  4. Kinetics. Mn lowers the eutectoid temperature and raises hardenability. The diffusion-controlled ferrite reaction slows, so at a given cooling rate the austenite forms pearlite, and finer pearlite.

Service advantages of pearlitic grey iron:

  • Higher strength and hardness than ferritic grey iron (up to about 350 MPa tensile, roughly 180 to 250 HB), with good wear resistance: cylinder blocks and liners, brake drums and discs, gears, machine-tool slideways.
  • The pearlitic matrix carries about 0.6 to 0.8% combined carbon, so wearing surfaces can be flame or induction hardened.
  • It keeps the virtues of grey iron: high damping capacity (machine beds), excellent machinability (graphite breaks chips and lubricates), high thermal conductivity (brakes), high compressive strength, low notch sensitivity, good castability and low cost.
  • Mn-stabilised pearlite resists decomposition, softening and growth in service at moderately raised temperatures.
pts: Why: the matrix is set at the eutectoid; Si and slow cooling favour ferrite + graphite; Mn tips it to pearlite (about 0.1% Mn ferritic up to 1.2% pearlitic)

Gives the rules: 1.7S + 0.15 for maximum ferrite, 3S + 0.35 for a pearlitic matrix
Free Mn dissolves in cementite, stabilises it and resists graphitisation
Mn raises carbon solubility in austenite and the combined carbon
Mn lowers the eutectoid temperature and raises hardenability, slowing the ferrite reaction: pearlite, and finer pearlite

12.html:
Choice of iron

Nodular (ductile, SG) cast iron, as cast or normalised to a pearlitic or ferrite-pearlite grade, or austempered (ADI) for the most heavily loaded, wear-exposed parts such as plough points and tines.

  • Strength with ductility. Spheroids are not notches (slide 3), so the iron gives about 490 to 800 MPa tensile with 8 to 15% elongation (slide 12) and survives the shock of soil and stones.
  • Economic mass production. It casts to near-net shape with good fluidity, in thin or thick sections, and its grades are set as cast by composition (Cu as a pearlite promoter), with no long heat treatment.
  • Against the others. Grey iron is weak and brittle (flakes, about 150 to 350 MPa, no elongation). White iron is hard but brittle and unmachinable, fit only for abrasion liners. Malleable iron is tough, and slide 20 shows farm parts made of it, but it must solidify white (thin sections only) and needs a long malleablising anneal near 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, which costs energy and furnace time.

Combined carbon after austenitising at 780^\circ\mathrm{C}

Given: nodular iron with 1.4% Si, austenitised at T_\gamma = 780^\circ\mathrm{C} and quenched.

Find: the combined carbon, that is the carbon dissolved in the matrix.

Solution. The austenite is in equilibrium with graphite, so its carbon is set by temperature and Si, not by the total carbon (book p 303; slide 13):

\begin{aligned} \%C_0 &= \frac{T_\gamma}{420} - 0.17\,\mathrm{Si} - 0.95 \\ &= \frac{780}{420} - 0.17(1.4) - 0.95 \\ &= 1.857 - 0.238 - 0.95 = 0.67\ \mathrm{wt\%} \end{aligned}

On quenching, this austenite becomes martensite with about 0.67% C. The rest of the carbon (about 2.9% in a typical 3.6% C iron) stays as graphite nodules.

Answer: combined carbon about 0.67 wt%. 780^\circ\mathrm{C} is a low austenitising temperature: the martensite is lower in carbon and softer than after the usual 870 to 900^\circ\mathrm{C} (0.95% C at 900^\circ\mathrm{C} for this iron), but it distorts less.
pts: Chooses nodular (ductile) iron, as cast, normalised or austempered (malleable iron justified by its use for farm parts, slide 20, earns 1.5)
Spheroidal graphite: no notch effect, so high strength with ductility and impact resistance (about 490 to 800 MPa)
Economy: near-net-shape casting in any section, grades set as cast, no long anneal
Rejects grey iron (weak, brittle flakes), white iron (brittle, unmachinable) and malleable iron (thin sections only, long anneal)
Recognises that the matrix carbon in equilibrium with graphite depends on temperature and Si: \%C_0 = T_\gamma/420 - 0.17\,\mathrm{Si} - 0.95
Substitutes correctly: 1.857 - 0.238 - 0.95
Final answer: about 0.67 wt% combined carbon, held in the martensite after quenching
Comments: a low temperature gives low-carbon, softer martensite; the rest of the carbon stays as graphite

1a.fix: Slide 22 says that above 490^\circ\mathrm{C} the gamma phase forms, and that the solubility limit of N in iron at 450^\circ\mathrm{C} is 5.7 to 6.1%. On the Fe-N diagram on the same slide, 490^\circ\mathrm{C} is only the Curie temperature of \gamma'-Fe4N, and austenite appears only above the eutectoid at 590^\circ\mathrm{C}; 5.7 to 6.1% N is the composition range of \gamma'-Fe4N, while ferrite itself dissolves at most about 0.1% N. Nitriding at 495 to 565^\circ\mathrm{C} is therefore ferritic, as slide 21 states.
1a.html:
Nitriding is ferritic and has no quench, so temperature and time alone set the case:

  1. Phases. Ferrite holds at most about 0.1% N; beyond it \gamma'-Fe4N (5.7 to 6.1% N) and then brittle \varepsilon-Fe2-3(N,C) form the white layer. Higher temperature, longer time and more carbon thicken it and favour \varepsilon, which spalls.
  2. Upper limit. Austenite forms above 590^\circ\mathrm{C} (Fe-N eutectoid), and above the prior tempering temperature the core softens and distorts: so 495 to 565^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  3. Hardness. Fine AlN and CrN give it; high temperature or long time coarsens them and softens the core, so hardness falls and life shortens.
  4. Depth. d \approx K\sqrt{t}, K rising steeply with temperature; 0.3 to 0.6 mm takes days, with diminishing return.
  5. Distortion and cost rise with temperature.

Hence the two-stage process: about 525^\circ\mathrm{C} for hardness, then 550 to 565^\circ\mathrm{C} for depth.
pts: Phase control: little N in ferrite, then \gamma' (5.7 to 6.1% N) and brittle \varepsilon; temperature, time and carbon set white-layer thickness and phase
Upper limit: below 590 degrees C (no austenite) and below the core tempering temperature; usual range 495 to 565 degrees C
Hardness: fine alloy nitrides coarsen at high temperature or long time, lowering hardness and shortening life
Depth d \approx K\sqrt{t} with K rising with temperature; slow at low temperature, diminishing return with time
Distortion and cost, and the two-stage compromise

1b.html:
Carbon diffuses interstitially, jumping between octahedral sites; carburising relies on its diffusion in austenite.

1. Temperature. D follows the Arrhenius law

D = D_0 \exp\left(-\frac{Q}{RT}\right)

For carbon in austenite D_0 = 2.3\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}} and Q = 148\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}: D = 5.9\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}} at 900^\circ\mathrm{C}, nearly double at 950^\circ\mathrm{C}. Case depth \approx K\sqrt{t} with K \propto \sqrt{D}, so a hotter cycle is much shorter. In BCC ferrite (Q = 80\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}) carbon diffuses faster, but ferrite dissolves only 0.022% C, so carburising is done in austenite.

2. Carbon content. D rises with dissolved carbon (slides 15, 18): at 900^\circ\mathrm{C} from about 0.8\times10^{-7} at 0.2% C to about 2\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm^2\,s^{-1}} at 1.0% C. Carbon expands the lattice and raises its own activity, lowering Q. D is highest in the carbon-rich surface, so calculations use an average D.

3. Other elements (slides 17-19):

  • Carbide formers Cr, Mn, Mo, Al, W lower D: they bind carbon, lower its activity and raise Q. Cr is strongest (1% Cr roughly halves D at 900^\circ\mathrm{C}); Mo is weaker.
  • Ni and Co raise D: they raise carbon activity and lower Q.
  • Si raises D at 900 to 970^\circ\mathrm{C} (over 20% for 0.2% Si, about 50% for 0.4% Si); the effect reverses slightly above about 1000^\circ\mathrm{C}.

So Cr-Mo steels need longer carburising than plain or Ni steels for the same case.

Carbide formers Cr, Mn, Mo, Al, W lower D (lower activity, higher Q); Cr strongest
Ni and Co raise D (higher activity, lower Q)
Si raises D at usual carburising temperatures (about 20 to 50%), with a slight reversal above about 1000 degrees C

1c.html:
Depth of hardened layer

The hardened depth is the distance from the surface to which the steel was austenitised during heating, and so became martensite on quenching. It is measured on a hardness traverse as the depth to a specified hardness (effective case depth).

For design it is set by the penetration (reference) depth \delta: the depth at which the induced current density falls to 37% (1/e) of its surface value:

J(x) = J_0\,e^{-x/\delta}, \qquad \delta = 5.03\sqrt{\frac{\rho}{\mu f}}\ \mathrm{cm}

with \rho the resistivity (\mu\Omega\,\mathrm{cm}), \mu the relative permeability and f the frequency (Hz). Heat goes as J^2, so about 86% of it is released within \delta; conduction makes the hardened depth slightly larger.

Controlling parameter: frequency

\delta \propto 1/\sqrt{f}. \rho and \mu are material properties that change during heating (\mu falls to 1 above the Curie point, 770^\circ\mathrm{C}; \rho rises to about 115\ \mu\Omega\,\mathrm{cm} at 900^\circ\mathrm{C}), so they cannot be set. The frequency is fixed exactly by the generator: four times the frequency halves \delta. For hot steel, \delta \approx 17 mm at 1 kHz, 5.4 mm at 10 kHz, 1.7 mm at 100 kHz and 0.85 mm at 400 kHz. Power density and heating time then trim the depth.

Sharper hardness change: laser

From the figure on slide 45, the laser case stays at about 800 HV to about 0.65 mm and drops to about 280 HV by 0.8 mm; the induction case falls gradually from about 770 HV to about 250 HV between about 0.5 and 2.5 mm.

Reason: the laser deposits its energy at the surface at very high power density in under a second, so the temperature gradient is very steep. The austenitised zone ends abruptly, the partly transformed transition zone is thin, and self-quenching gives fine martensite. Induction generates heat throughout \delta and conducts it inward for seconds: a gentle gradient and a wide transition zone.
pts: Defines the hardened depth as the depth austenitised and turned to martensite, measured to a specified hardness
Defines \delta as the depth where the induced current falls to 37% (1/e) of the surface value, J = J_0 e^{-x/\delta}
States \delta = 5.03\sqrt{\rho/\mu f} cm with the meaning and units of each symbol
About 86% of the heat within \delta; hardened depth slightly larger by conduction
Frequency is the controlling parameter: \delta \propto f^{-1/2}, while \rho and \mu are material properties
Gives values or the Curie-point effect (for example 5.4 mm at 10 kHz, 0.85 mm at 400 kHz for hot steel)
Power density and heating time as secondary controls
Laser gives the sharp change, with the profile values from the figure
Reason: steep thermal gradient, short time, narrow transition zone and self-quench, against volumetric heating and conduction for seconds in induction

2a.html:
Tool steel is any carbon or alloy steel made to shape other materials by cutting, forming, machining, battering or die casting, or to cut wood, paper, rock or concrete. It carries about 0.5 to 1.5% C, often with the carbide formers W, Cr, V and Mo; its hardness, wear resistance, toughness and hot hardness come from hard carbides in a martensitic matrix. The AISI groups are W, O, A, D, S, T, M, H and P (slide 7).

Purposes of heat treatment:

  1. Give a structure suitable for machining or cold forming (annealing to fine pearlite or spheroidised carbide).
  2. Relieve residual stresses from forging, machining and grinding (stress relief below Ac1).
  3. Homogenise the structure, with fine, uniformly distributed globular carbides (spheroidising).
  4. Dissolve harmful grain-boundary carbides and refine the grain (normalising).
  5. Harden: austenitise to dissolve the right amount of carbide, then quench to martensite for hardness and wear resistance.
  6. Temper: remove retained austenite, precipitate carbides of controlled size (secondary hardening, red hardness), and restore toughness and dimensional stability.
pts: Defines tool steel: carbon or alloy steel for cutting and shaping other materials, about 0.5 to 1.5% C, hardness and wear resistance from carbides of W, Cr, V, Mo

Purpose: relief of residual stresses below Ac1
Purpose: homogenised structure with fine globular carbides
Purpose: dissolve intergranular carbides and refine the grain (normalising)
Purpose: hardening to martensite with controlled carbide dissolution for hardness and wear resistance
Purpose: tempering to remove retained austenite, control carbides (secondary hardening) and restore toughness

2c.html:
As-quenched tool steel is martensite, retained austenite (RA) and undissolved carbides. Tempering below Ac1 runs in three steps for carbon steels and five for highly alloyed tool steels (slides 25-26):

  1. 50 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C}, \varepsilon-carbide. Carbon leaves the martensite as fine coherent \varepsilon-carbide (\mathrm{Fe_{2.4}C}) and tetragonality falls; the volume contracts. Softening is delayed and quench stresses relax.
  2. 200 to 350^\circ\mathrm{C}, cementite. \varepsilon-carbide dissolves and \mathrm{Fe_3C} rods and films precipitate at the lath boundaries; the matrix becomes ferrite and hardness falls.
  3. RA destabilisation (from about 150^\circ\mathrm{C} in carbon steels, 450^\circ\mathrm{C} in high-alloy steels). Carbides precipitate from the RA, lowering its C and alloy content and raising its M_s. It transforms to bainite during the hold or to fresh martensite on cooling: a volume expansion that grows with the RA fraction, and a hardness gain.
  4. From about 500^\circ\mathrm{C}, highly alloyed steels with carbide formers. Carbon passes from cementite to alloy carbides: cementite dissolves and fine \mathrm{M_2C} and MC of Mo, W and V precipitate (secondary hardening), with a large volume expansion (slide 26).
  5. From 600^\circ\mathrm{C} to Ac1. The carbides coalesce and coarsen and the matrix recovers: softening towards an annealed structure, with a volume contraction.

Consequences. The fresh martensite from step 3 is brittle and must itself be tempered, so tool steels are tempered at least twice, and three times for high-carbon HSS, complex hot-work dies, large moulds and gauges (slide 29). The volume changes of steps 1 and 3 to 5 must be allowed for in the dimensions machined before hardening.

3a.fix: Slide 21 of Ch 5 (and the course book p 281) states bright annealing in hydrogen or dissociated ammonia "below -50^\circ\mathrm{C}" and that a "slightly higher temp" gives a thin green oxide. The -50^\circ\mathrm{C} is the dew point of the atmosphere (its moisture content), and the green \mathrm{Cr_2O_3} forms when the dew point is not low enough. 3a.html:
Bright annealing

Bright annealing is annealing (for austenitic grades, solution annealing at 1010 to 1120^\circ\mathrm{C}) in a protective pure dry hydrogen or dissociated ammonia (75\%\ \mathrm{H_2} + 25\%\ \mathrm{N_2}) atmosphere, with cooling in the same gas, so that the parts come out bright and oxide-free with no pickling. The dew point must be below -50^\circ\mathrm{C} and the parts clean and dry: \mathrm{Cr_2O_3} is so stable that only a very dry gas keeps it from forming. With a wetter gas a thin green \mathrm{Cr_2O_3} film forms that is hard to remove.

Martensite in solution-treated austenitic stainless steel

Solution treatment keeps all C and Cr dissolved, so the austenite is as stable as it can be, yet still metastable:

M_s(^\circ\mathrm{C}) = 1302 - 42\,\mathrm{Cr} - 61\,\mathrm{Ni} - 33\,\mathrm{Mn} - 28\,\mathrm{Si} - 1667\,(\mathrm{C}+\mathrm{N})

For a typical 304L, M_s \approx -200^\circ\mathrm{C}, while M_d is above room temperature (M_{d30} \approx 25^\circ\mathrm{C}).

  • On cooling: below M_s (cryogenic cooling) austenite shears to \alpha' without diffusion (athermal).
  • By deformation (the usual case): below M_d, plastic strain supplies the extra driving force. Stacking faults on \{111\}_\gamma build \varepsilon martensite (HCP, non-magnetic, volume -0.81\%); \alpha' (BCC, ferromagnetic, volume +2.57\%) nucleates at shear-band and \varepsilon intersections: \gamma \to \varepsilon \to \alpha'.
  • Low stacking-fault energy, low temperature and more strain raise the \alpha' fraction (V_{\alpha'} = A_1\varepsilon^B V_\gamma, B \approx 3).
  • If the steel is later sensitised, Cr-depleted zones next to the grain boundaries have a higher M_s, so \alpha' forms there first.

3b.html:
Martensite forms only from austenite, so the steel must be fully austenitic at the hardening temperature. Above 14% Cr this failed because:

  1. Cr closes the \gamma loop. Cr, a ferrite (BCC) stabiliser, shrinks the \gamma field of carbon-free Fe-Cr to a closed loop ending at about 12 to 13% Cr near 1000^\circ\mathrm{C}. Outside the loop the steel is ferritic at every temperature: nothing transforms, so it stays ferritic on quenching.
  2. Too little carbon for the chromium. C, N and Ni widen the loop: 13% Cr needs over 0.15% C (austenitised at 950^\circ\mathrm{C} or above), 17% Cr over 0.3% C and at least 1100^\circ\mathrm{C}. Raising Cr without raising C left the alloy outside the loop.
  3. Carbon locked in carbides. More Cr stabilises \mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6}; at too low an austenitising temperature it stays undissolved, so less C is in solution and the loop shrinks further.
  4. As-cast \delta-ferrite. On the Schaeffler diagram (0.5% Si and Mn assumed), 13Cr-0.2C (\mathrm{Cr_{eq}} \approx 13.8, \mathrm{Ni_{eq}} \approx 6.3) lies in the martensitic-alloy box (just on the M + F side of the martensite line, so little ferrite), which ends at \mathrm{Cr_{eq}} \approx 15.5; 17Cr-0.2C (\mathrm{Cr_{eq}} \approx 17.8) falls outside it, in the A + M + F field with about 20 to 30% ferrite. Cr-rich interdendritic zones of a casting turn ferritic first.

Remedy: raise C (440C: 17% Cr, 1.1% C), add about 2% Ni (431) or N, and austenitise near 1100^\circ\mathrm{C}.

3c.html:
Intergranular corrosion (IGC) is localised attack along the grain boundaries while the grains themselves are hardly attacked; whole grains can drop out and the metal loses strength.

Cause in austenitic stainless steel: sensitisation. Heating in, or slow cooling through, about 425 to 815^\circ\mathrm{C} (welding, stress relief, service) precipitates Cr-rich \mathrm{M_{23}C_6} (\mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6}) on the grain boundaries. Carbon diffuses fast but Cr slowly, so a thin band next to each boundary falls below about 12% Cr and cannot stay passive. In an acid it dissolves; in welds this is weld decay in the heat-affected zone a few mm from the fusion line.

Remedies

  1. Solution annealing: 1010 to 1120^\circ\mathrm{C} (316: at least 1040^\circ\mathrm{C}) dissolves the carbides and restores Cr; then cool fast (water) through 900 to 450^\circ\mathrm{C}. It also cures sensitised parts and welds.
  2. Extra-low carbon (L grades): 304L, 316L, 317L with at most 0.03% C. Too little C for harmful carbide; they survive up to about 2 h in 425 to 815^\circ\mathrm{C} and need no quench, but not long service there.
  3. Stabilised grades: Ti at least 5 \times \%\mathrm{C} (321) or Nb(+Ta) at least 10 \times \%\mathrm{C} (347, 348). TiC and NbC are more stable than \mathrm{Cr_{23}C_6}, so C is tied up and Cr stays in solution.
  4. Stabilising anneal: 845 to 955^\circ\mathrm{C} for up to 5 h after solution annealing precipitates MC instead of \mathrm{M_{23}C_6}; L grades with Mo: 885^\circ\mathrm{C} for 2 h before stress relief at 675^\circ\mathrm{C}.
  5. Avoid the sensitising range: stress relieve only at 425 to 550^\circ\mathrm{C} (carbides very slow), use low heat input and fast cooling in welding, and avoid carbon pickup (clean parts, no carburising atmosphere).
  6. Alloy choice: N alloying (316LN) restores the strength lost with low C; duplex grades resist IGC because Cr diffuses fast in ferrite and depleted zones heal.

5.html:
Tungsten steels: properties induced by heat treatment

W forms extremely hard, stable carbides (\mathrm{W_2C}, \mathrm{M_6C}), dissolves slightly in cementite, stabilises ferrite and segregates strongly (about 90% hot reduction is needed to break it up). Heat treatment unlocks these effects:

  1. Annealing (spheroidising, slow cool): soft, machinable ferrite with spheroidal \mathrm{M_6C}.
  2. Hardening from a very high temperature (T1 high-speed steel, 18W-4Cr-1V: 1260 to 1300^\circ\mathrm{C}, after two-stage preheating because of the low conductivity) dissolves part of the W carbides. Quenching gives martensite, retained austenite and undissolved carbides: high hardness and wear resistance (W is next to V), and fine grain because the carbides pin the boundaries.
  3. Multiple tempering at 540 to 565^\circ\mathrm{C}: \mathrm{W_2C} precipitates and retained austenite transforms on cooling, giving secondary hardening (63 to 65 HRC) and red hardness: the edge stays hard at 550 to 600^\circ\mathrm{C}. Hence T-type high-speed steels and H21 to H26 hot-work dies.

W has a high hardenability factor, but its carbides withdraw carbon, so large additions lower the net hardenability.

Weathering steels for structures in Bangladesh

Weathering steel holds about 0.1% C, 0.2 to 0.5% Cu, 0.5 to 1.0% Mn, 0.05 to 0.15% P, 0.15 to 0.9% Si, sometimes Cr and Ni. In wet-dry cycles Cu, P and Cr enrich a dense, adherent, self-healing rust layer (patina) that blocks water and oxygen, so after a few years corrosion becomes very slow and the steel is used unpainted.

  • Climate: hot and humid, with monsoon rain and dry winters, gives the wet-dry cycling the patina needs; ordinary steel rusts fast and needs repainting every few years.
  • Use: a riverine country needs thousands of steel bridges, plus railway wagons, transmission towers and sheds. Unpainted weathering steel saves painting cost and traffic closures, lowering life-cycle cost; as an HSLA grade (yield about 345 MPa) it also allows lighter sections.
  • Limits: not for permanently wet or buried members or salt-laden coastal zones (Chattogram, Cox's Bazar), where a Ni-rich grade or paint is needed; details must drain water.

7.html:
Why full annealing suits hypoeutectoid steel

Full annealing gives maximum softness, ductility and machinability, refines a coarse as-cast, forged or overheated structure and relieves stresses.

  1. Heating to \mathrm{A_3} + 30 to 40^\circ\mathrm{C} makes the whole section single-phase austenite. Both the old ferrite and the pearlite transform, so the structure is completely renewed as fine austenite grains. The small margin limits grain growth.
  2. Slow furnace cooling then gives proeutectoid ferrite followed by coarse pearlite: the softest ferrite-pearlite structure.
  3. The proeutectoid phase of a hypoeutectoid steel is soft, ductile ferrite, so slow cooling from the single-phase field is harmless.
  4. In a hypereutectoid steel the same route deposits a continuous brittle cementite network on the grain boundaries, so those steels are only heated just above \mathrm{A_1} or spheroidised instead. Heating a hypoeutectoid steel only between \mathrm{A_1} and \mathrm{A_3} would leave the old ferrite untransformed and the structure uneven.

Full-annealing temperature of AISI 1140

Given: C 0.44, Mn 1.0, Si 0.1, S 0.1 wt%; Ni, Cr, V, Mo nil.

Find: \mathrm{A_1}, \mathrm{A_3} and the annealing temperature.

Solution:

\begin{aligned} \mathrm{A_1} &= 723 - 10.7(1.0) + 29.1(0.1) = 715^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ \mathrm{A_3} &= 910 - 203\sqrt{0.44} + 44.7(0.1) = 910 - 134.7 + 4.5 = 780^\circ\mathrm{C} \\ T_{\text{anneal}} &= \mathrm{A_3} + (30\ \text{to}\ 40) = 810\ \text{to}\ 820^\circ\mathrm{C} \end{aligned}

S has no term; it is tied up as MnS, which makes 1140 free machining. With the formulas as printed in the course (203 \times \%\mathrm{C} and 20.7 \times \%\mathrm{Mn}), \mathrm{A_3} = 825^\circ\mathrm{C}, the anneal 855 to 865^\circ\mathrm{C} and \mathrm{A_1} = 705^\circ\mathrm{C} (see Correction).

Schedule: heat to about 815^\circ\mathrm{C}, soak at least 20 min per cm of section (100 min for a 50 mm bar), furnace cool at 20 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C}\,\mathrm{h^{-1}} to below \mathrm{A_1} (about 650^\circ\mathrm{C}), then air cool. Result: about 46% ferrite and 54% coarse pearlite.

Answer: \mathrm{A_3} \approx 780^\circ\mathrm{C}, so full anneal at about 810 to 820^\circ\mathrm{C}; \mathrm{A_1} \approx 715^\circ\mathrm{C}.

8.html:
Normalised 1.5% C steel: harder and tougher

Annealed (\mathrm{A_1} + 30 to 50^\circ\mathrm{C}, about 760^\circ\mathrm{C}, furnace cooled): the proeutectoid cementite (about 12%) is not dissolved, and slow cooling thickens it into a thick, continuous network around coarse pearlite colonies. Cementite is brittle with a very low tensile strength (about 5000 psi, 34 MPa), so the network is a continuous crack path: low strength, low toughness, poor machinability.

Normalised (about 50^\circ\mathrm{C} above Acm, about 1000^\circ\mathrm{C}, still-air cooled):

  1. Above Acm all cementite, the network included, dissolves into homogeneous austenite.
  2. Air cooling leaves little time for proeutectoid cementite: it forms only as thin, broken films. Undercooled austenite also transforms directly to pearlite (quasi-eutectoid), so less proeutectoid cementite forms at all.
  3. The pearlite forms at a lower temperature, so its interlamellar spacing and colony size are finer, and the grains are finer.

Finer pearlite and grain size give the higher hardness and strength (normalised tensile strength about 1000 MPa against about 620 MPa annealed near 0.9% C, slide 18). With no continuous brittle path, a crack must cross tough pearlite, so toughness is also higher. Above about 0.9% C the normalised steel is tougher as well as stronger (slide 17).

Cluster-like pearlite around large ferrite grains (normalised hypoeutectoid steel)

This is an inhomogeneous normalised structure (book Fig 2.24). Causes:

  1. Austenitising temperature too low or soak too short. Some ferrite is not transformed, or the austenite keeps its carbon gradients: low-C regions (old ferrite) and high-C regions (old pearlite). On cooling the old ferrite grows into large grains and the carbon-rich pockets turn into pearlite clusters. Fast heating raises \mathrm{Ac_3} and makes this worse.
  2. Overheating or too long a hold. Coarse austenite grains offer few boundary sites, so the ferrite that forms grows large and pushes carbon into the last austenite, which becomes pearlite pockets between the ferrite grains.
  3. Slow cooling of heavy sections or packed loads gives ferrite time to grow.
  4. Segregation or banding (Mn, P) and alloying elements slow carbon diffusion, so a normal soak does not homogenise the austenite.

Remedy: \mathrm{A_3} + 50 to 60^\circ\mathrm{C}, hold 60 + D min, and for alloy steels a lower temperature with a longer hold.
pts: Annealed 1.5% C steel: heated only just above A1 and furnace cooled; thick continuous cementite network around coarse pearlite
Network weakness: brittle cementite with very low tensile strength (about 5000 psi) forms a continuous crack path, so low strength and toughness
Normalised: heated above Acm (about 1000 degrees C), all cementite dissolved, still-air cooling
Air cooling gives thin, broken cementite (and quasi-eutectoid pearlite), so toughness rises
Finer pearlite spacing and grain size give higher hardness and strength (about 1000 against 620 MPa near 0.9% C)
Draws the Fe-Fe3C temperatures and the two microstructures
Pearlite clusters reason 1: low austenitising temperature or short soak leaves ferrite or carbon gradients, so large ferrite grains and carbon-rich pearlite pockets form
Reason 2: overheating or long hold gives coarse austenite, large ferrite grains and pearlite pockets
Reasons 3 and 4: slow cooling of heavy sections; segregation, banding or alloying slow homogenisation; with the remedy

9.html:
Readings from Figure 1 (an isothermal diagram, although the question calls it a cooling curve): nose about 0.85 s at 540^\circ\mathrm{C}, bainite below about 550^\circ\mathrm{C}, M_s \approx 225^\circ\mathrm{C}, M_f \approx 130^\circ\mathrm{C}. Bainite at 400^\circ\mathrm{C}: start 4.4 s, finish about 100 s; at 300^\circ\mathrm{C}: start about 95 s, finish about 2060 s. (By formula B_s = 630 - 45(0.6) = 603^\circ\mathrm{C} and M_s = 520 - 320(0.9) - 50(0.6) = 202^\circ\mathrm{C}; the figure values are used.)

Plan: 25% upper bainite at 400^\circ\mathrm{C}, 25% lower bainite at 300^\circ\mathrm{C}, then the remaining 50% austenite to martensite. The fraction between start (1%) and finish (99%) follows the Avrami equation:

X = 1 - \exp(-k t^n), \qquad n = \frac{\ln(4.605/0.01005)}{\ln(t_f/t_s)}
  • 400^\circ\mathrm{C}: n = 1.95, so 25% forms at t \approx 25 s.
  • 300^\circ\mathrm{C}: n = 1.99; 25% would need 512 s and 50% 796 s. By additivity the 25% already formed counts as 512 s, so the hold is 796 - 512 \approx 285 s.

Schedule:

  1. Heat slowly and preheat at 600 to 650^\circ\mathrm{C}: \mathrm{CE} \approx 0.9 + 0.6/5 \approx 1.0, very crack sensitive.
  2. Austenitise at about 790^\circ\mathrm{C}, just above A_{cm} (about 770^\circ\mathrm{C}), so all cementite dissolves as the diagram assumes; soak 60 + D min.
  3. Quench into a salt bath at 400^\circ\mathrm{C}, faster than (727 - 540)/0.85 \approx 220^\circ\mathrm{C\,s^{-1}}, to miss the nose.
  4. Hold about 25 s at 400^\circ\mathrm{C}: 25% upper bainite.
  5. Transfer within 2 to 3 s (the reaction runs at about 1.7% per second) to a second bath at 300^\circ\mathrm{C} and hold about 285 s (5 min): 25% lower bainite.
  6. Quench in oil or water to room temperature. The remaining 50% passes M_s and M_f, both above room temperature, and becomes martensite.
  7. Temper at 150 to 200^\circ\mathrm{C} for 1 to 2 h, well below the bainite temperatures.

Expected hardness from the scale of Figure 1: 0.25(42) + 0.25(52) + 0.5(66) \approx 56 HRC as quenched.
